'''''Davidia involucrata''''', '''dove tree''',<ref name="Rushforth">{{cite book | last=Rushforth | first=Keith | title=Trees of Britain and Europe | publisher=Trafalgar Square Publishing | publication-place=London | date=1999 | isbn=0-00-220013-9 | pages=661–663}}</ref> '''ghost tree''', '''handkerchief tree''', or '''pocket handkerchief tree''' is a medium-sized [[deciduous]] tree in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Nyssaceae]].<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=''Davidia involucrata'' Baill. | website=Plants of the World Online | date=2020-06-02 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:430593-1 | access-date=2025-06-14}}</ref><ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 9 January 2017}}</ref>  It is the only living species in the [[genus]] '''''Davidia'''''. It was previously included with [[Tupelo (tree)|tupelo]]s in the dogwood family, [[Cornaceae]].<ref name=APW>{{cite web | url = http://www.mobot.org/mobot/research/APweb/orders/cornalesweb.htm#Cornales | title = Angiosperm Phylogeny Website - Cornales | publisher = [[Missouri Botanical Garden]] | access-date=28 August 2023}}</ref> Fossils of the species have been found in the [[Upper Cretaceous]].

==Taxonomy==
''Davidia involucrata'' is the only member of its [[genus]], but two varieties differing slightly in their leaves were formerly often distinguished, ''D. involucrata'' var. ''involucrata'', with the leaves densely pubescent on the underside, and ''D. involucrata'' var. ''vilmoriniana'', with glabrous or only thinly hairy leaves.<ref name=FoC>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200014694 |title=''Davidia involucrata'' |author=Haining Qin & Chamlong Phengklai |work=Flora of China |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden, St. Louis, MO & Harvard University Herbaria, Cambridge, MA |accessdate=28 April 2013}}</ref> These are now known to intergrade and are no longer considered distinct;<ref name="POWO"/> earlier reports of differing [[chromosome]] numbers between the two (which if true would prevent interbreeding)<ref name="Rushforth"/> proved erroneous due to the difficulty of counting numerous small chromosomes accurately,<ref name="JLS">{{cite journal | last=He | first=Zi-Can | last2=Li | first2=Jian-Qiang | last3=Wang | first3=Heng-Chang | title=Karyomorphology of ''Davidia involucrata'' and ''Camptotheca acuminata'', with special reference to their systematic positions | journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society | volume=144 | issue=2 | date=2004 | issn=1095-8339 | doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2003.00241.x | pages=193–198 | url=https://academic.oup.com/botlinnean/article-lookup/doi/10.1111/j.1095-8339.2003.00241.x | access-date=2025-06-14| url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="TSO">{{cite web | title=''Davidia involucrata'' | website=Trees and Shrubs Online | date=2025-06-13 | url=https://www.treesandshrubsonline.org/articles/davidia/davidia-involucrata/ | access-date=2025-06-14}}</ref> with the species now confirmed to have 2n = 42 chromosomes.<ref name="JLS"/>

==Description==
It is a moderately fast-growing tree, growing to {{convert|20|-|25|m|0|abbr=on}} in height, with toothed, alternate, ovate-cordate leaves superficially resembling those of a [[Tilia|lime]] (''Tilia''), except that they are symmetrical, lacking the lop-sided base typical of lime leaves; the leaves are mostly 10–20 cm long and 7–15 cm wide.

''Davidia involucrata'' is best known for its [[inflorescence]] that features two large, white [[Bract|bracts]], the lower almost twice the size of the upper,<ref>{{cite book | last= Hogan | first= Sean | date=2004 | title= Flora - The Gardener's Bible | location= Willoughby, New South Wales | publisher= Global Book Pub. Pty. Ltd. | pages= 476-477 with photo | isbn= 1-74048-097-X }}</ref> surrounding a purplish-red flower [[Head (botany)|head]]. The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''involucrata'' means "with a ring of bracts surrounding several flowers".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref> The true flowers form a tight head about 1–2 cm across, each flower head with a pair of large (12–25 cm), pure white [[bract]]s at the base, performing the function of petals in attracting pollinators. The inflorescences hang in long rows beneath the horizontal branches, and appear prolifically in late spring. On a breezy day, the bracts flutter in the wind like white [[dove]]s or pinched handkerchiefs; hence the English names for this tree.

The fruit is a very hard [[nut (fruit)|nut]] about 3 cm long surrounded by a green husk about 4 cm long by 3 cm wide, hanging on a 10 cm stalk. The nut contains 3–6 seeds. According to Turner and Wasson, these seeds can take as long as three years to [[germinate]].<ref>{{cite book | last1=Turner | first1= R.J. Jr. | last2= Wasson | first2= Ernie | date= 1999 |title= Botanica | location= not given | publisher= Barnes & Noble | page= 292 | ISBN= 0760716420 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Davidia involucrata'' is [[native plant|native]] to [[South Central China|South Central]] and Southeast China. It grows in montane mixed forests.<ref name="POWO"/>

==History==
The genus ''Davidia'' is named after Father [[Armand David]] (1826–1900; "Père David"), a French [[Vincentian Family|Vincentian]] missionary and keen naturalist who lived in China. David first described the tree in 1869 as a single tree found at over {{convert|2000|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} altitude, and sent dried specimens to Paris; in 1871, [[Henri Baillon]] described it as a new genus and species.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Baillon|first=Henri|date=1871|title=Davidia involucrata|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9bUXAAAAYAAJ&pg=PP9|journal=Adansonia|volume=10|pages=115|via=Google Books}}</ref><ref>[http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/1758.pdf "E. H. Wilson's First Trip to China"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100729012411/http://arnoldia.arboretum.harvard.edu/pdf/articles/1758.pdf |date=29 July 2010 }}, by William H. Gardener, in ''Arnoldia'', the quarterly journal of the [[Arnold Arboretum]]; published May 3, 1972 (vol. 32, no. 3, pp. 103–115; introduction by Gordon P. DeWolf, Jr.</ref>

The British plant hunter [[Augustine Henry]] again found a single tree, this time in the Yangtse Ichang gorges and sent the first specimen to Kew Gardens. The plant collector [[Ernest Henry Wilson]] was employed by Sir Harry Veitch to find Henry's tree but arrived to find that it had been felled for building purposes; however, he later found a grove of the trees overhanging a sheer drop.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.arboretum.harvard.edu/wilsons-search-for-davidia-involucrata/|title=E. H. Wilson's search for Davidia involucrata|last=Glasser|first=Larissa|date=27 November 2018|website=Library Leaves - Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190416170226/https://www.arboretum.harvard.edu/wilsons-search-for-davidia-involucrata/ |archive-date=16 April 2019 |access-date=2 October 2019}}</ref> Returning to Britain, Wilson's boat was wrecked, but he managed to save his ''Davidia'' specimens,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.lmi.org.uk/medical_society/16/16Martin.pdf |title=Evolve 360 |access-date=2 July 2010 |archive-date=16 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716102942/http://www.lmi.org.uk/medical_society/16/16Martin.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> one of which survives today in the Arnold Arboretum.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-11-27 |title=E. H. Wilson's search for ''Davidia involucrata'' |url=https://arboretum.harvard.edu/stories/e-h-wilsons-search-for-davidia-involucrata/ |access-date=2022-04-26 |website=Arnold Arboretum |language=en-us}}</ref>

==Fossil record==
The oldest probable fossils of ''Davidia'' are [[permineralized]] fruit from the [[Upper Cretaceous]] ([[Campanian]]) [[Horseshoe Canyon Formation]] of [[Dinosaur Provincial Park]] near [[Drumheller]], [[Alberta]], [[Canada]]. Those fruit are smaller than those of ''D. involucrata'' and have fewer [[locule]]s, but are otherwise similar in morphology to the extant genus.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.palaeobotany.org/page/living-fossils/davidia-involucrata/ |title=International Organisation of Palaeobotany (IOP) - ''Davidia'' - the Dove Tree and its fossil record |access-date=18 December 2015 |archive-date=24 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151224165622/http://www.palaeobotany.org/page/living-fossils/davidia-involucrata |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2009, B. I. Pavlyutkin described [[Miocene]] fossils in [[Primorsky Krai]] and assigned them to a new species in the genus ''Davidia''.<ref>{{citation | doi = 10.1134/S0031030109030137 | journal = Paleontological Journal | issn = 1555-6174 | volume = 43 | issue = 3 | date = May 2009 | pages = 339–344 | title = Leaf and fruit remains of ''Davidia'' (Cornales) from the Nezhino flora (Miocene of Primorye) | author = B. I. Pavlyutkin | bibcode = 2009PalJ...43..339P | s2cid = 83645195 }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
The species was introduced from China to Europe and North America in 1904, and is a popular [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] tree in parks and larger gardens. Most trees in cultivation are of the glabrous form, which has proved much better able to adapt to the climatic conditions in Europe and North America.

This tree<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web|title=''Davidia involucrata'' AGM|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/5364/Davidia-involucrata/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|accessdate=23 May 2020}}</ref> and the cultivated [[variety (botany)|variety]] ''D. involucrata'' var. ''vilmoriniana''<ref>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/96467/i-Davidia-involucrata-i-var-i-vilmoriniana-i/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Davidia involucrata'' var. ''vilmoriniana''
| accessdate = 6 February 2018}}</ref>  have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 29 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 6 February 2018}}</ref>
